rewritten_text:
The first time I caught Tom alone, I asked what he'd had in mind during the escape—what he meant to do if everything worked and he managed to free a Black man who was already free. He said his plan all along, once we got Jim out safely, was to take him downriver on the raft and have adventures all the way to the river's mouth. Then we'd tell him he was free, bring him home in style on a steamboat, and pay him for his lost time. We'd send word ahead and gather all the Black people around, so they could march him into town with torches and a brass band. He would be a hero, and so would we. But I reckoned things had turned out just as well as they were.

We got Jim out of his chains in no time. When Aunt Polly, Uncle Silas, and Aunt Sally learned how well he'd helped the doctor nurse Tom, they made a great fuss over him. They saw he was comfortable, gave him all the food he wanted, let him enjoy himself, and gave him nothing to do. We brought him up to the sickroom and had a lively talk. Tom gave Jim forty dollars for patiently playing prisoner for us and doing it so well. Jim was nearly beside himself with pleasure, and burst out:

‘There now, Huck! What did I tell you? What did I tell you back on Jackson's Island? I told you I had a hairy chest, and what that was a sign of. And I told you I'd been rich once and would be rich again. Now it's come true, and here's the money! There now! Don't argue with me—signs are signs, remember that. I knew I'd be rich again as sure as I'm standing here this very minute!’

Then Tom went on talking and talking. He said the three of us should slip away some night, get our supplies together, and spend a couple of weeks or so having wild adventures among the Native Americans in the Territory. I said that suited me fine, but I had no money to buy supplies. I reckoned I couldn't get any from home either, because Pap had probably been back by now, taken everything from Judge Thatcher, and drunk it all away.

‘No, he hasn't,’ Tom said. ‘It's all still there—six thousand dollars and more. And your pap hasn't ever come back since.’

You won't know anything about me unless you've read a book called The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that don't matter. Mr. Mark Twain made that book, and mostly he stuck to the truth. Some things he stretched a little, but the greater part was true. That's nothing much. I never met anybody that didn't lie sometime or other, except maybe Aunt Polly, or the widow, or perhaps Mary. Aunt Polly—that's Tom's Aunt Polly—and Mary and the Widow Douglas are all in that book, which is mostly truthful, with a few stretchers thrown in, as I already said.

Now, here's how that book ends: Tom and me discovered the money the robbers had hidden in the cave, and we came out rich. Each of us got six thousand dollars, every bit of it gold. Piled together, it was an amazing heap of money. Well, Judge Thatcher took charge of it and invested it at interest, and each of us got a dollar a day the whole year through—more than anybody could know how to spend. The Widow Douglas took me in as her son and said she'd sivilize me; but being shut in the house all the time was hard, seeing how drearily proper and regular the widow was about everything. So when I couldn't bear any more, I cleared out. Back I went to my old rags and my sugar barrel, feeling free and contented. But Tom Sawyer tracked me down and told me he was starting a robber band, and I could belong if I went back to the widow and behaved respectably. So back I went.

The widow cried over me and said I was a poor lost lamb, along with a good many other names, though she didn't mean any harm. She got me into those new clothes again, and all I could do was sweat and sweat and feel squeezed up tight. Then the same old business started over. She rang the supper bell, and you had to turn up punctual. Once you reached the table you couldn't just begin eating; first you had to wait while she bent her head and mumbled over the food, although there wasn't really anything wrong with it—except that each thing had been cooked separate. It's different in a barrel of scraps: everything mixes together, and the juice goes passing round, and it all tastes better.

After supper she brought out her book and taught me about Moses and the Bulrushers, and I was mighty eager to hear all about him. But presently she happened to mention that Moses had been dead a long while. After that I lost interest, because dead people don't count for much with me.

The following day he remained indoors, spending, in fact, nearly all his time in his own room, sick with a frantic dread of death and yet unconcerned with life itself. The sense of being pursued, trapped, hunted down was beginning to possess him. A mere stirring of the tapestry in the wind made him tremble. Dead leaves blowing against the leaded windows seemed like his own squandered resolutions and desperate regrets. Whenever he shut his eyes, the sailor's face reappeared, peering through the mist-clouded glass, and horror seemed to press its hand against his heart again.

Yet perhaps only his fancy had summoned vengeance from the darkness and placed those dreadful shapes of punishment before him. Real life was confusion, but imagination possessed a terrible logic. Imagination made remorse follow at the heels of sin; imagination gave every crime its deformed offspring. In the ordinary realm of facts, evil went unpunished and goodness unrewarded. The strong were granted success, the weak burdened with failure. That was everything. Besides, if a stranger had been skulking about the house, surely a servant or keeper would have noticed him. If footprints had appeared in the flowerbeds, the gardeners would have mentioned them. Yes, it was nothing but fancy. Sibyl Vane's brother had not returned to murder him. He had gone away aboard his ship, to perish in some wintry sea. From that man, at least, he was secure. Why, the fellow did not know his identity, could not possibly know it. His youthful mask had rescued him.

And still, if it had been no more than an illusion, how dreadful to reflect that conscience could summon such terrifying spectres, clothe them in visible shapes, and set them moving before one's eyes! What kind of existence awaited him if, night and day, the shadows of his crime watched from quiet corners, jeered from hidden places, whispered into his ear while he sat at a feast, or roused him with frozen fingers in his sleep? As this thought stole through his mind, terror drained his face, and the air seemed suddenly to grow colder. Oh, in what a frenzied hour of madness had he murdered his friend! How hideous even the recollection of that scene! It all unfolded before him once more. Every dreadful detail returned with a fresh intensity of horror. From time's black cavern arose the image of his sin, terrible and wrapped in scarlet.
